**Verdict:** No. Paul Graham would tell you not to start a startup while you're enrolled. Keep building the side project on your own time, and decide on a full-time move only if it grows into something that takes over your life.

**Based on:** said it (confidence: high). He answered this question directly, in a 2014 talk ([[yt-ii1jcLg-eIQ]], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ) and again in his August 2026 essay ([[web-c75e015ff81a]], https://paulgraham.com/prepare.html).

**Why they'd say it**
- He's blunt about college: "Do not start a startup in college." ([[yt-ii1jcLg-eIQ]] @ 18:56, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=1136s) He also says 20 isn't the optimal age: "though starting a startup could be a good thing to do at some point, 20 is not the optimal time to do it."
- Waiting costs you little: "You're not sacrificing anything if you forego starting a startup at 20, cuz you'll be more likely to succeed if you wait." ([[yt-ii1jcLg-eIQ]] @ 21:12, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=1272s)
- Being a student and running a startup don't mix: "Running a startup is incompatible with being a full time student." ([[web-c75e015ff81a]])
- He wants you to protect the side project, because the best startups start there: "start as side projects, because they're always such outliers that your conscious mind would reject." ([[yt-ii1jcLg-eIQ]] @ 25:41, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=1541s)
- The exception is a project that takes off on its own, like Facebook: "Then you face the choice of either running with it or not, and maybe it's reasonable to run with it." ([[yt-ii1jcLg-eIQ]] @ 21:12)

**What's changed:** The 2026 essay is less dismissive of side projects. It asks universities to give students free time for them, since some become startups. Microsoft and Meta both started during Harvard's reading period. But it also says the choice is hard: "Are the students just supposed to abandon them? Because it's either that or drop out." ([[web-c75e015ff81a]]). The vault records this as a shift in emphasis, not a reversal ([[tensions]]). The essay is addressed to universities, so it doesn't say outright what a student should do.

**What would change their answer:** A project that "takes over an alarming percentage of your life" ([[yt-ii1jcLg-eIQ]] @ 43:15). At that point he allows that running with it may be reasonable, even though it means leaving school.

**Caveat:** The vault flags that PG's advice to students comes from the founder of an accelerator that funds them, so he has a stake in the YC model ([[profile]], @ 44:55).

**Verdict:** Yes, he'd tell you to go, but for a while, not for good. He says "should," not "need": "Yes, you should. You can go there for a bit and then come back, but you should at least go." ([0:36](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=36s) [[yt-QHJkUw31YX8]])

**Based on:** said it (confidence: high). He addressed this exact question in his April 2026 talk in Stockholm.

**Why he'd say it**
- **Peers:** "You get the best peers. And in fact, the talent pool expands in two dimensions. The people are better, and there's also a lot more of them." ([1:09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=69s))
- **Pace:** "Things also tend to move faster in the big centers because the people are better, they're more confident, and that's more decisive. They also tend to egg one another on." ([3:53](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=233s))
- **The bigger effect is on you:** "the biggest advantage of moving to one of these centers is not what it does for you, but what it does to you." ([8:19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=499s)) Seeing known big fish up close makes your goal feel hard rather than impossible.

**Caveats he gives himself**
- **Self-interest:** "I know, I know it will sound like I'm talking my own book at this point, but honestly, this is so true, I have to say it." He then says the "optimal way" to go for a bit and come back is YC ([17:16](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=1036s)).
- **His one hard number:** startups that go back home after YC are "only about half as likely to become unicorns" ([18:57](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=1137s)). That's YC's internal data, with no method shown. He also says it's full of selection bias, since it measures founders' confidence and determination as well as the location.
- **Altman (July 2026) is less firm.** Moving to the Bay Area was the best way to find co-founders, and he thinks that's probably still good advice, but says he has less intuition for it now ([[startups/location/should-you-move-to-silicon-valley]]).

**For Stockholm:** He doesn't write the city off. He says a hub needs "a place founders want to live and a critical mass of them," and that founders who go and come back help the city: "as long as you do actually come back, that's one of the best things you can do to help Sweden to help Stockholm thrive as a startup hub." ([16:10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QHJkUw31YX8&t=970s))

**What would change his answer:** His argument is built for ambitious people working in a field that has a center. He gives painting, math and movies as examples and says "every field has one center." If your field has no such center, the case is weaker. That's my reading of his conditions; he doesn't address it. The location pages in the vault don't cover cost of living, family, or whether remote collaboration weakens the peer argument, so the vault has nothing on those.

**Verdict:** Seibel would say the months of pitching are the problem, not the deck. Stop treating the raise as a sales process to polish. Put your time into growth until investors are the ones chasing you, and cap the pitching instead of letting it run.

**Based on:** said it. The principle comes from the October 2026 "Dalton + Michael" episode and his 2019 MVP talk. Applying it to your months of pitching follows from that (confidence: high). The vault has no seed-specific source, and the episode doesn't discuss your situation.

**Why he'd say it**
- Investors chase what's working: "if you can invest that time in making your company something that investors will chase after versus decksmithing, you're you're playing into the odds versus playing out of the odds." ([yt-7TU636F @ 10:03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7TU636F_yVQ&t=603s))
- His own fundraise: Justin.tv spent about eight months trying to raise. When it was clear the money wasn't coming, with two months of runway left, they went for profitability. He says they got more done in those two months than in the months of pitching. ([@ 6:44](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7TU636F_yVQ&t=404s))
- He counts the cost: "if you just think about how much time is wasted, it's like a drag on the industry." ([@ 7:18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7TU636F_yVQ&t=438s))
- It isn't new: "spending all that time on a pitch deck is not as valuable as spending your time building anything that you can give to a customer." ([yt-1hHMwLxN6EM @ 11:11](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM&t=671s))

**What to take from it** (my reading, not his)
- Ask how much leverage you have: how badly you need this round and how long you can wait. The episode defines leverage as the ability to walk away.
- Treat the follow-up meetings as a signal. The episode, without attributing it to either host, describes investors who keep taking meetings to hold an option on a company that might take off. If the meetings aren't turning into a decision, that's the pattern to check.
- Set a date to decide, either to close the round or to switch to making the company profitable. Seibel doesn't give a deadline. His Justin.tv story shows what happens when the money stops coming.

**What would change his answer:** The advice assumes your company isn't yet pulling in users or revenue, and you didn't say whether it is. If it is growing fast and investors are still hesitating, this vault doesn't say what he'd do next.

**Caveats:** The fundraising material is one 2026 episode. It's sponsored by Standard Capital, an investor fund that Caldwell co-hosts and partners in. "Investors chase 80–90% of deals" comes from an informal question Seibel put to investors, not from data. The Justin.tv and Socialcam stories are from an earlier era of venture.

**Verdict:** Stop paying lawyers to trade letters over stock that's worth nothing. Seibel would have you agree a no-fault split: your co-founder gives back nearly all of his vested stock (under 2%, since you're inside the first year), you both sign clean paperwork, and you wind the company down instead of spending more time on it.

I read "it's clearly over" as the company winding down, with your co-founder as the one leaving. Their reasoning in plain words: before product-market fit the stock has created no value, so the fight is over nothing, and the lawyers are the ones who profit from the anger.

**Based on:** said it. The breakup, the lawyers and the numbers are addressed directly. The shutdown extends his line that when the odds are zero, you should "stop wasting time."

**Why they'd say it**
- Worthless stock means the fight is over nothing: "in a situation where you're having a co-founder breakup and the stock is worth nothing, paying lawyers a bunch of money makes no sense." ([[yt-s1YszjhzQ6U]] @ 11:36; https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s1YszjhzQ6U&t=696s)
- Lawyers profit from it: "a lawyer can suck up infinite amount of your ... anger and monetize it." (@ 12:07)
- Stop wasting time: "when you really know the probability of success is zero, most important thing is to stop wasting time." (@ 9:26)
- The number at your stage: "even if you vested, like get down to under 5% of the company, if it's within the first year, under 2%." (@ 18:39) and "Under a year, 1%, 2%, sometimes less than 1%." (@ 21:22)
- It can be cheap: "you could do that whole thing in a week and spend like $2,000." (@ 18:39)
- Don't let a referee become the judge: "If you're using someone to mediate this, don't make them the judge." (@ 19:46). Caldwell, in the same episode: "Don't try to ruin the other person. Don't try to ruin the reputation." (@ 13:42)

**This isn't "no lawyers":** "I would call the lawyers. But just just be smart and nice about it and it'll work out." (@ 22:26) My read is one lawyer scoped to the paperwork, not two lawyers in a letter war.

**Check two things first**
- **The percentages assume the company keeps going.** The rule applies when the company "is going to continue operating" (@ 14:47), because the leaver's equity is meant to motivate the people who stay. If the company is shutting down, there's no one left to motivate, so the percentage is mostly a bargaining chip. Cash and debt matter more. He warns that a leaving founder can end up with debt on a company "not worth anything" (@ 12:39). Check whose name the bills and any personal guarantees are in.
- **Is it the product or the customer?** His test before giving up: "hold the problem you're solving tightly, hold the customer tightly, hold the solution you're building loosely." ([[yt-1hHMwLxN6EM]] @ 3:19; https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM&t=199s) If the customer and problem are still real and you've tried only one solution, that's a pivot question, not a shutdown.

**What would change their answer**
- Misconduct. "if your co-founder is breaking the law, doing something unethical, killing people, none of this applies." (@ 21:54) Caldwell carves out felonies too (@ 13:42).
- Value. If there's cash, revenue or a live buyer, the stock isn't worth nothing, and the "don't spend on lawyers" logic becomes a fight about real money.
- The company keeps going. Then the 2% and 5% numbers apply in full, and the equity should stay with the people who stay.

**Caveats**
- Most speaker attributions in this episode are inferred from context, so they're medium confidence. Seibel's takeaways from 20:50 onward are clearly his.
- The vault notes that Standard Capital, a Series A fund Caldwell co-founded, sponsored this episode. Its "keep equity with the people who stay" argument favors the company continuing.
- I'm not a lawyer. Share cancellation or buyback, IP assignment and dissolution are jurisdiction-specific, and the vault doesn't cover them. Have a competent lawyer draft them once.

**Correction first:** Garry Tan didn't say this. Sam Altman did, at YC's Startup School 2026 (July 28, 2026), in a conversation that Tan hosted. The vault has no statement from Tan about the premium or the gap.

**Verdict:** Altman credits network effects. Being in YC puts you among the people you'll later build with, that network compounds, so the premium has grown and the lead over the next option has widened. He gives no numbers.

**Based on:** said it (Sam Altman, not Garry Tan)

**What he said**
- "I think the premium on doing YC is bigger now than it's like ever been before." "The distance between like YC and second place is has expanded. And this is a reminder of the power of network effects." ([[yt-ZIaOBAjvc38]] @ 16:56, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZIaOBAjvc38&t=1016s)

**How he gets there**
1. Co-founder matching was the bottleneck. Five or ten years ago, the main limit on how many good startups YC could fund was helping talented people find their people. Moving to the Bay Area was "clearly right" ([[yt-ZIaOBAjvc38]] @ 16:25).
2. Being in the Bay Area is still probably the best way to find your people, because you get "lucky chances and collisions" ([[yt-ZIaOBAjvc38]] @ 16:56).
3. Getting into those networks early matters because the payoff "takes a long time to compound" ([[yt-ZIaOBAjvc38]] @ 17:28). The widening gap is his evidence for network effects.

**Caveats**
- He hedges the first point: "I still think that's probably good advice, although I feel like I have less of an intuition for it now" ([[yt-ZIaOBAjvc38]] @ 16:56).
- He flags his own position: "I can say this, Gary probably can't." He doesn't say why. My reading is that Tan, as YC's head, wouldn't make that boast himself.
- He's a former YC president speaking at YC's own event, so he has a stake in the claim. "Second place" is never named, and no data is given.
- The transcript is auto-generated captions, so the exact wording may be slightly off.

**Closest thing Tan said:** Tan doesn't claim the premium or the gap. He calls the "loose network and the spirit of helping each other" "a huge part of what has made YC work and the broader startup ecosystem," then moves on to AGI ([[yt-ZIaOBAjvc38]] @ 23:35, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZIaOBAjvc38&t=1415s).

**Verdict:** The vault doesn't support that premise. Jessica Livingston never says early YC backed the most aggressive or ruthless founders, and nothing in the vault suggests she thinks ruthlessness wins. The one "ruthless" from her describes the VC investors of that era, and she sets YC against them:

> "I was soft and sensitive at a time when investors tended to be hardened and aggressive and I'll throw in ruthless" ([[yt-8d-cApFHjeY]] @ 17:44, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8d-cApFHjeY&t=1064s)

She goes on to say she cared how founders were feeling, and counseled them through strained relationships and co-founder disputes ([[yt-8d-cApFHjeY]] @ 18:18).

**Based on:** the vault contradicts the premise. The inference below follows from what she said, with low confidence.

**What she did say about the founders YC picked**
- **Earnestness:** "from the beginning I was very careful about only funding earnest people" ([[yt-8d-cApFHjeY]] @ 14:51, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8d-cApFHjeY&t=891s). Early on she was "pretty rigid about this," and she turned down applicants she judged conceited ([[yt-8d-cApFHjeY]] @ 15:27).
- **Co-founders:** she asked "what was the relationship between the co-founders like" ([[yt-8d-cApFHjeY]] @ 14:51).
- **Potential over résumé:** "we had to judge the founders not by what they were but what they could turn into" ([[yt-8d-cApFHjeY]] @ 16:35).
- **Boldness, not aggression:** "you do need a certain amount of boldness to work on ideas that most people would consider stupid and to keep going when you're ridiculed or ignored" ([[yt-8d-cApFHjeY]] @ 25:45, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8d-cApFHjeY&t=1545s).

**The nearest "winners are the formidable ones" idea is Paul Graham's, not hers.** He defines formidable as "someone who gets what they want in any situation," and says investors want formidable founders because "if they get what they want, you get what you want" ([[yt-5bxp78i96S8]] @ 9:57, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5bxp78i96S8&t=597s). The vault calls "formidable" their shared private language, but the definition is framed from an investor's side.

**How we get there (inference, low confidence)**
1. Her stated rule is to back earnest founders with good co-founder relationships, and to screen out conceit ([[yt-8d-cApFHjeY]] @ 14:51, @ 15:27).
2. She never addresses ruthlessness as a trait, so this is an extrapolation.
3. She would most likely say the founders who win are earnest, determined and bold, and that conceit is a reason to say no. Her own "soft and sensitive" framing makes it unlikely she'd pick ruthlessness as the criterion, but the vault doesn't say that outright.

**What would change this:** a source the vault doesn't hold. It cites two of her talks, from 2018 and 2024. Her 2024 talk describes the founders as "unconventional, you know independent-minded" ([[yt-6u4JVz7iQTY]] @ 19:17, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6u4JVz7iQTY&t=1157s), which is about thinking differently, not aggression. If you have a source where she says YC chose the most aggressive founders, it would need to go into the vault before I could cite it.

The only other "ruthless" in the vault is about cutting MVP features, not founders, so that's probably not where the idea came from.
